You understand and build new words at B2 level with prefixes (des-, in-/im-, re-, pre-, sobre-, sub-, anti-) and suffixes (-ción, -miento, -dad, -eza, -ura for nouns; -dor, -ista, -ero for people; -ble, -oso, -ivo for adjectives; en-/a- … -ecer for verbs), so you can expand your vocabulary without a dictionary.
Books enrich those who read them.
She thanked him with great tenderness.
In Triana it gets dark later than in Bucharest.
To recognise prefixes of negation and opposition: des- (deshacer), in-/im-/i- (inútil, imposible, irreal), anti- (antiniebla).
To use prefixes of repetition, time and degree: re- (releer), pre- (prever), sobre- (sobrevivir), sub- (subrayar).
To form abstract nouns from verbs and adjectives: -ción, -miento, -dad, -eza, -ura, -ez.
To form nouns for people and adjectives: -dor/-dora, -ista, -ero/-era; -ble, -oso/-osa, -ivo/-iva.
To form verbs from adjectives and nouns with en-/a- + -ecer / -ar: envejecer, enriquecer, acercar, alargar.

Friday, 2 October, in Ecaterina's flat in Bucharest. Tomorrow "Lampa aprinsă", the Romanian edition, is launched. Ecaterina is checking the last page again with Ana. Rosa Elena is drawing on the rug and listening.
There's a word that still doesn't convince me: "reencuentro". In Romanian, "reîntâlnire" sounds like a school reunion.
But it's exact: "re-" plus "encuentro". Finding each other again.
Exact isn't always beautiful. And then there's "desesperanza". It's not the same as "desesperación".
Despair screams. Hopelessness sits down in silence and stops waiting. "Des-" takes away the hope; it doesn't add noise.
So if I turn off the lamp, do I "unlamp" it?
Not yet. But it's very well made. It's impossible not to understand it.
Almost. You say "traductora". But for the books of my life, I like "traducedora" better.
The stress always falls on "-ción", and in the plural the written accent disappears: ca-SIÓN → ca-SIO-nes, ilu-SIÓN → ilu-SIO-nes.
Adjectives in -ble are stressed on the syllable before it: i-ne-VI-ta-ble, in-ol-vi-DA-ble, im-pres-cin-DI-ble.
When the prefix "des-" is followed by a vowel, the "s" joins the next syllable: de-sa-MOR, de-sor-DEN, de-sa-pa-re-CER.
hacer → deshacer, amor → desamor, esperanza → desesperanza, gustar → disgustar
negation (im- before p/b, i- before l/r)
útil → inútil, posible → imposible, legal → ilegal, real → irreal
"in-" becomes "im-" before "p" and "b" (imposible, imborrable) and "i-" before "l" and "r" (ilegal, irresponsable, with "rr").
2. Prefixes of repetition, time and degree
again: to reread; to find each other again; to redo
before: to foresee; prehistory; to prevent
over: to survive; the time after a meal; supernatural
"Re-" can also intensify: «rebueno», «requetebién» (very good, colloquial). And "recién" + participle = just: recién casados, recién llegado, recién hecho.
traducir → traducción, decidir → decisión, emocionar → emoción
agradecer → agradecimiento, nacer → nacimiento, sufrir → sufrimiento
amable → amabilidad, feliz → felicidad, libre → libertad
triste → tristeza, tierno → ternura, viejo → vejez
soñar → soñador, novela → novelista, libro → librero
Nouns ending in -ción, -sión, -dad, -tad, -eza, -ura are feminine: la traducción, la libertad, la tristeza, la ternura. Those ending in -miento are masculine: el agradecimiento.
olvidar → inolvidable, creer → increíble, leer → legible
cariño → cariñoso, orgullo → orgulloso, miedo → miedoso
decidir → decisivo, crear → creativo, expresar → expresivo
viejo → envejecer, rico → enriquecer, noche → anochecer, oscuro → oscurecer
cerca → acercar, largo → alargar, corto → acortar
If you know the root, you can guess the meaning: «enrojecer» = to blush (rojo), «entristecer» = to sadden (triste), «ensanchar» = to widen (ancho).
Se sienta en silencio y deja de esperar
Before the wedding, Faustino sends Marta a little "dictionary" of his life. Notice the prefixes and suffixes.
Dear Marta, you ask me for words for the ending of your novel. Here are a few. For sixty years I was a solitary bookseller and an incorrigible bachelor.
I knew sadness, but never hopelessness, because there was always a new book to open. Loneliness aged me less than you think.
Now I am a newly engaged man of eighty-seven, which is an unpredictable situation and, according to my doctor, hardly advisable.
If you need one last word for the ending, I suggest this one: gratitude. It is long, but everything I don't know how to say fits inside it. Faustino.
¿Qué palabra le propone a Marta para el final?

"Lampa aprinsă", the Romanian edition of Ecaterina's book, came off the press on Thursday, 1 October. The Bucharest publisher sent the first box to her home by courier, and Ecaterina opened it alone, at the living-room table, with Andrés's tortoiseshell glasses and the little lamp lit, although it was ten in the morning. The book was the same as the Spanish one, with the same photo by Andrei on the cover, the empty drawer, but the title was in Romanian. Ecaterina opened it at the dedication. She had translated it herself, word for word, and it was the only sentence in the book she had never changed: "Pentru A., care a lăsat lumina aprinsă."

Translating herself had been the strangest experience of her professional life. For forty years she had translated others, and she had always known that her job was to disappear behind them. Now she couldn't disappear, because the author was her. She told Ana that the hardest part hadn't been the long sentences, but the small words, the ones that in Spanish were made of other words. "Reencuentro", "desesperanza", "inolvidable", "desamor". In Spanish a prefix was enough to turn a word inside out. In Romanian, sometimes, it took a whole sentence, and at other times the word existed but sounded different, like a familiar house with the furniture moved around.

On the eve of the launch, Ana came to help her with the final check, and Rosa Elena came with her. The girl sat on the rug with her pencils and spent the afternoon listening to the two women argue about whether "desesperanza" was the same as "desesperación". Ecaterina explained to Ana that it wasn't: despair screams, and hopelessness sits down in silence and stops waiting. Rosa Elena raised her head and asked whether, when she turned off the lamp, she "unlamped" it. Ana told her that word didn't exist. Ecaterina told her not yet, but that it was very well made, because it was impossible not to understand it.

From that afternoon on, Rosa Elena never stopped inventing words. If Costel drove the truck, he was a "camionador". If Grandpa Gheorghe told stories, he was a "historiero". If Mrs Florica made three-tier cakes, she was a "tartista". Ecaterina explained to her which ones existed and which didn't, and why: that you say "camionero", with "-ero", like "librero" and "panadero"; that "historiador" was something else, someone who studies the past; and that "tartista" didn't exist, but "pastelera" did. Rosa Elena wrote it all down in her school notebook, on a page she had titled, in crooked letters, "Real words and fake words".

The launch of "Lampa aprinsă" was on Saturday, 3 October, at a bookshop in central Bucharest with an inner courtyard full of chestnut trees. It was smaller than the one in Madrid, but Ecaterina said afterwards it had been the hardest, because for the first time she was being listened to in her own language by people who had known her all her life. There were her former colleagues from the publishing house, the neighbour from the third floor, two university professors who had studied with her in the sixties, Ana and Mihai, Mr Dan and his wife, Mrs Florica with her husband, and Costel, who had swapped a shift to be able to come and had put on the only tie he owned.

Ecaterina read the lamp chapter in Romanian. When she reached the last sentence her voice broke, as in Madrid, and she had to stop. This time it wasn't Marta who finished reading it, because Marta was in Madrid. It was Costel. He stood up from the third row, came to the table, picked up the book very carefully, as if it were burning, and read the sentence aloud, slowly, in his trucker's voice. Then he gave it back to Ecaterina and sat down again, red to the ears. People applauded for a long time. Ecaterina told him afterwards that he had been the best reader she had ever had. Costel replied that he had been the most nervous.

There was one question from the audience Ecaterina didn't expect. It came from a young woman, a translation student, who wanted to know whether translating yourself was easier or harder than translating someone else. Ecaterina thought for a moment. She answered that it was impossible to say, because when she translated someone else she could blame the author for everything she didn't like, and when she translated herself she had no one to blame. But she added that she had discovered one thing: that there were sentences she had only been able to write in Spanish, and that in Romanian she understood them better. As if the foreign language had helped her say them, and her own had helped her believe them.

That same night, Ecaterina packed her suitcase. She was leaving for Spain on Tuesday, first to Madrid, for the plaque's anniversary, and then to Seville, for the wedding. She packed two copies of "Lampa aprinsă", one for Lola and one for doña Remedios, although neither of them knew Romanian. She packed the blue dress she had bought for the wedding, after discussing it with Ana for a week, and the silk shawl her mother had given her in 1975. And at the last minute she packed a little cloth bag of walnuts from Grandpa Gheorghe's tree, which Costel had brought her from the village that afternoon with a message: "For the bride and groom. May they grow old together, even though they've already started."

On Monday, the day before the trip, Mr Dan dropped by Ecaterina's with a folder under his arm. Preparing for the November session, he had discovered that in the reading comprehension paper there were always words he didn't know, and that almost all of them were made of others he did know. So he had made a new table: prefixes in one column, suffixes in another, and in the third, examples taken from Ecaterina's book. "Inolvidable", "desesperanza", "reencuentro", "enriquecer". He asked her if the table was right. Ecaterina checked it with her tortoiseshell glasses and told him it was missing only one word: "imprescindible". And that he was.

On 7 October, at twelve, it was exactly one year since they had unveiled the bronze plaque on calle de las Huertas. This time there were no speeches or journalists. Only the usual people came: Lola, in a new apron; Begoña, who said she happened to be passing by, although she had the big camera hanging from her shoulder; Andrei and Lucas, who had taken the morning off; Marta, with the manuscript of her novel in a blue folder; and Ecaterina, who had arrived from Bucharest the night before. They stood in front of the plaque for a while, without saying anything. That morning someone had left a small bunch of yellow flowers at the foot of the green sign.

Nobody found out who had left the flowers. Lola said that since the book came out, things appeared at the foot of the plaque almost every week: flowers, notes, once a candle, another time a book by Cortázar with an anonymous dedication. She collected them at night and kept them in a box behind the counter, so as not to throw them away. Ecaterina asked her how many there were by now. Lola told her she had stopped counting in March, when they passed a hundred. Then she took her inside and showed her the box. Ecaterina read a few notes. One said simply: "Thank you for leaving the light on. I left it on too, and it came back." It was unsigned.

Ecaterina gave Lola her copy of "Lampa aprinsă". Lola leafed through it with great respect, without understanding a word, and said it was the most beautiful book she would never be able to read. Then she put it on the back shelf, under the lamp, next to the first Spanish copy. Now there were two identical books, in two languages, under the same light. Begoña, who had said nothing all morning, came over and took a photo of the two books. Just one. Then she slung the camera over her shoulder and left, saying she had work to do. Lucas told Andrei quietly that Begoña had no work on Wednesday mornings.

That afternoon, Andrei showed Ecaterina two things. The first was his new contract, as a staff photographer, which he had signed on the 1st and carried folded in his wallet, as if it were a winning lottery ticket. The second was a photo: Faustino's back walking away along the Cuesta de Moyano, with the red beret. He told her Begoña had said it was the cover of a novel. Marta, who was there, took the photo, looked at it for a moment without saying anything and put it in the blue folder, on top of the manuscript. Andrei asked her if that meant yes. Marta answered that it meant she wasn't giving it back.

Marta, meanwhile, confessed to Ecaterina that she had a problem with her novel. Inés had told her that the best endings are written after things happen, and she had listened: she had two hundred and forty pages written and the last chapter blank. But now she was afraid the real wedding would be so beautiful that no invented ending could live up to it. Ecaterina told her that was impossible, because reality is never entirely beautiful: there's always someone who arrives late, a shoe that pinches, a speech that's too long. She suggested she write that. That imperfection, well told, was what made a story unforgettable.

A few days before the wedding, Faustino sent Marta a handwritten letter, which he called "my dictionary". It was a list of words with which, according to him, his life could be told. He wrote that for sixty years he had been a solitary bookseller and an incorrigible bachelor; that he had known sadness, but never hopelessness, because there had always been a new book to open; that loneliness had aged him less than people thought. And that now he was a newly engaged man of eighty-seven, an unpredictable situation and, according to his doctor, hardly advisable. At the end he suggested one last word for the ending of the novel: gratitude.

On Thursday, 15 October, Ecaterina, Marta and Andrei took the AVE to Seville. Lucas couldn't go, because someone had to open the stall on Sunday, and he had promised Faustino he would never close it on a Sunday, not even on the Sunday of his wedding. Begoña didn't go either; she said weddings put her in a bad mood. But on Friday morning a parcel from Madrid with no sender arrived at doña Remedios's house. Inside was a framed photo: the two books, the Spanish and the Romanian, under the lamp at El Mostrador. On the back, in small, cramped handwriting, she had written a single sentence: "Not bad. B."

In Seville, Triana was decked out as if for a neighbourhood festival. Doña Remedios's bookshop had its window decorated with white flowers and with all the books of her life standing upright, open, as if they were listening. The neighbours had hung shawls from the balconies along the street. Curro had tuned his guitar three times. Pilar and Manuel had come from Cádiz with Manuel's parents, who wanted to meet the woman who was marrying their in-law's friend. And doña Remedios's daughter, the one who had told her in June that nobody got married at her age, had turned up with an enormous hat and very red eyes.

The night before the wedding, Curro and Andrei took Faustino for a walk along the bank of the Guadalquivir, because doña Remedios had said she didn't want to see him until the altar. Faustino walked slowly, hands behind his back, looking at the lights on the other side of the river. When they reached the bridge he stopped and confessed to them that he was afraid. Not of getting married, he said, but of not being up to it. Of being an inexperienced husband, at his age, with the clumsiness of a beginner. Curro, who was twenty, told him that all husbands were inexperienced on the first day. Faustino laughed. He said it was the wisest sentence he had ever heard from someone so young.

The wedding was on Saturday, 17 October, at six in the evening, in the church of Santa Ana, the oldest in Triana. Ecaterina was doña Remedios's witness. Andrei was Faustino's witness, because Faustino had said he wanted beside him someone who knew how to look without talking. Doña Remedios arrived on Curro's arm, in a cream-coloured dress and with the fan for special occasions. Faustino was waiting for her at the altar with the red beret in his hand, because the priest had warned him he couldn't wear it inside the church. He was so nervous he was crumpling it like a handkerchief.

As Ecaterina had predicted to Marta, not everything was perfect. The priest arrived ten minutes late, because his motorbike had broken down. Faustino's new shoes pinched, and halfway through the ceremony he discreetly took them off under the pew, although everyone saw. And when the moment of the rings came, Curro, who had them, couldn't find them: he had put them in the guitar case, which was in the sacristy. For two endless minutes, the whole church waited in silence. Doña Remedios said aloud that, after eighty-four years, two more minutes didn't matter at all. The whole church burst out laughing.

Marta, sitting in the fourth row, wrote everything down in her notebook, with a smile she couldn't wipe off. She wrote down the priest's motorbike, the shoes under the pew, the rings in the guitar case, doña Remedios's sentence and the church's laughter. Ecaterina saw her from the altar and winked at her. When the rings finally appeared, Faustino and doña Remedios didn't put them on right away. First they gave each other something else: she gave him the original lamp bookmark, the one Andrés had drawn in 1958; he gave her the framed five-hundred-peseta note. The two things they had kept longest in their lives.

Then they put on the rings, and the priest declared them husband and wife. Faustino put on his red beret as soon as they came out of the church door, as if he had been waiting for that moment all his life. In the square the neighbourhood women were waiting for them with rice and rose petals, and Curro began to play sevillanas. The newlyweds danced the first one, slowly, he without shoes and she with her fan, in front of all of Triana. Pilar was crying in Manuel's arms. Doña Remedios's daughter was crying under her hat. And Ecaterina, who had promised herself she wouldn't cry that day, cried too, but in a new way: without sadness.

Dinner was in the bookshop's courtyard, under an orange tree, at long tables lent by the neighbours. There was jamón, gazpacho, fried fish, an enormous tortilla made by Carmen, who had come from Bucharest on Friday with Juan, and a three-tier cake ordered from the best pastry shop in the neighbourhood. In the middle of the table, doña Remedios placed the little bag of walnuts from Grandpa Gheorghe. Ecaterina translated Grandpa's message for everyone: that they should grow old together, even though they had already started. Faustino laughed so hard he had to take off his glasses. He said Grandpa Gheorghe was the wisest man he had ever met, and the worst mus player.

There was also a video. Ana had sent it to Ecaterina that morning, and Andrei projected it onto the white wall of the courtyard when night fell. It showed Rosa Elena on Grandpa Gheorghe's porch, with her camera round her neck, and behind her Grandpa, very serious, in his Sunday cap. The girl said in Spanish, slowly, a sentence she had prepared for a week: "Dear señor Faustino, dear doña Remedios: I wish you an unforgettable life, a house without sadness and many books to reread." Then she turned to Grandpa, who said, in his three-word Spanish: "Por fin. Salud." The whole courtyard applauded.

Before the speech, Ecaterina paid her debt. She went up to Faustino with a parcel wrapped in newspaper, the way he wrapped his books, and told him it was the interest. Inside was a copy of Neruda's "Twenty Love Poems", an old 1961 edition she had found in a second-hand bookshop in Bucharest, with her dedication on the first page: "For Faustino, who charged me five hundred pesetas and gave me back a life. With interest, E." Faustino opened it in the middle, at poem twenty, and read it in a low voice, just for himself. Then he closed it and told Ecaterina the debt was settled. For ever.

Very late, when the guests were starting to leave, Faustino asked for silence and said a few words. It was a short speech, because, as he said, at his age long speeches were reckless. He said he had spent sixty-three years selling books to strangers, and had never known why he did it, until that year. That he had done it so as to be on the Cuesta de Moyano on the day a Romanian translator would pass by with a debt of five hundred pesetas. Because without that debt he would never have really known Andrés, or Ecaterina, or gone to Bucharest, or come back to Triana, or found Remedios. "Everything is made of everything," he said.

Doña Remedios said nothing. She took Faustino's hand, took off his beret, put it on the table next to the walnuts, and kissed him on the forehead, with great tenderness, in front of everyone. Then she turned to Ecaterina and told her she had something for her. She gave her an envelope. Inside was an old iron key. She explained it was the key to the room upstairs in the bookshop, the one overlooking the orange tree, and that from that day on it was hers, for whenever she wanted to come to Triana to write, or not to write. Ecaterina asked her why. Doña Remedios answered: "Because we all need a drawer that isn't empty."

Marta wrote the last chapter of "La librera de Triana" on the AVE back to Madrid, on Monday, 19 October, between Córdoba and Ciudad Real. She wrote it in one go, in two and a half hours, without lifting her head from the laptop. She put in the priest's motorbike, the shoes under the pew, the rings in the guitar case and the church's laughter. She put in Faustino's speech, the iron key and Grandpa's walnuts. And she ended the novel with the word Faustino had suggested in his dictionary. When she typed the final full stop, she closed the laptop, looked out of the window at the olive trees of La Mancha and cried silently all the way to Atocha.

Ecaterina, sitting beside her, didn't ask her anything. She took out her notebook and, on the last page, under Rosa Elena's sentence about wishes and letters, wrote the list of words she was taking with her from that month: reunion, newlyweds, gratitude, tenderness, unforgettable. Then she added one more, which didn't exist in any dictionary, in Spanish or in Romanian, and which a five-year-old girl sitting on a rug in Bucharest had given her: "deslampar". Underneath she wrote its definition: "To turn off a lamp knowing that tomorrow it will be lit again." Andrei, across the aisle, took a photo of her without her noticing.
¿Quién terminó de leer la última frase en la presentación de Bucarest?
¿Qué mandó el abuelo Gheorghe para los novios?
Una bolsita de nueces de su nogal
¿Qué se dieron los novios antes de los anillos?
El marcapáginas de la lámpara y el billete de quinientas pesetas
¿Qué le regaló doña Remedios a Ecaterina?
La llave de la habitación de arriba de la librería

The newlyweds danced in the square.
It's impossible not to understand it.
